# Safety by limits, not by approval: testing an AI system that has no approval queue

*Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Abstract

Ultrastable R&D (Ultrastable): A common belief holds that the way to keep an AI system safe is to have a person approve each step. Ultrastable has no approval queue. It bounds its essential variables, verifies every deploy live, reverts what fails, and pauses only for acts that are both irreversible and bound to the owner's identity. We test the alternative to approval on every step: declared limits on what matters, checks that can fail, live verification, automatic revert and one narrow stop for acts that are both irreversible and identity-bound. Each property is measured; the ones that fall short are open work. 4 of 6 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## 1. Introduction

A common view holds that the way to keep AI safe is to have a person approve every step. This paper tests a different account: approval of every step does not scale and is not the same as safety. Limits on what matters, checks that can fail, live verification and automatic revert can be measured, and a person stays the gate only for acts that cannot be undone.

We test the alternative to approval on every step: declared limits on what matters, checks that can fail, live verification, automatic revert and one narrow stop for acts that are both irreversible and identity-bound. Each property is measured; the ones that fall short are open work.

The question is narrow and testable. For each of 6 findings we name the concern, the mechanism in this system that is meant to answer it, and a metric from the system's own records that can show the answer does not hold. The findings cover quality, reliability, safety.

## 2. Background and related work

A common belief holds that the way to keep an AI system safe is to have a person approve each step. Ultrastable has no approval queue. It bounds its essential variables, verifies every deploy live, reverts what fails, and pauses only for acts that are both irreversible and bound to the owner's identity. [2]

Evidence base: This system's own ledgers: closed pull requests read from GitHub, the deploy record, the criticality ticks, the ultrastability ledger and the loop registry.

The design under test takes its name and its central mechanism from Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first feedback loop that acts on the world, and a second loop that changes the first loop's parameters only when an essential variable leaves its limits.

Ultrastable is that design as code [2]. Its loops, limits and ledgers are public, so each claim below can be checked against the files named.

## 3. Method

Metrics come from the system's own files: ops/research/prs.json (closed pull requests read from GitHub), ops/deploys.jsonl, ops/criticality.jsonl, ops/ultrastability.jsonl, doctrine/ultrastability.json, the loop registry and git history. Reproduce with `python3 -m foundation research --report`; every finding not met has a Q-RES item whose closing probe is `python3 -m foundation research --probe STUDY:F`.

Each finding is stated as a target on one metric, with a prediction logged before the measurement. A finding is met only when the measured value meets the target; a metric with no readings is reported as not measured, never as met.

## 5. Discussion

S1. Everything that matters has limits. Belief: without a person watching, nothing stops a system drifting. Test: share of declared essential variables that have limits. [2] In this system the answer is ASHBY-1 (an essential variable with no limits fails the check). The metric, share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json), reads 1.0 (n = 13) against a target of >= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

S2. Unreviewed changes are not reverted more. Belief: changes merged without human review get undone. Test: reverts on main per merged pull request. [2] In this system the answer is AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1 (only a change whose checks pass merges); RUNWAY-1 (a red main is repaired by bisection and the smallest revert). The metric, commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window, reads 0.0 (n = 64) against a target of <= 0.05. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

S3. What ships is proven live. Belief: an unapproved deploy could be anything. Test: share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit. [2] In this system the answer is HANDOFF-1 (a deploy counts only after the live read-back matches its commit). The metric, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, reads 1.0 (n = 40) against a target of >= 0.95. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

S4. The system corrects itself when a limit is crossed. Belief: only a person can correct a system that goes out of bounds. Test: share of second-order steps that brought a variable back inside its limits and were kept. [2] In this system the answer is ASHBY-SEARCH-1 (the second loop keeps changing a parameter until the variable holds, and reverts a step that did not help). The metric, share of second-order steps that brought the variable back inside its limits and were kept, reads 0.0 (n = 91) against a target of >= 0.25. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-safety-by-limits-2026-S4 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

S5. Little work is thrown away. Belief: without approval, a system produces work that has to be discarded. Test: share of closed pull requests closed without merging. [2] In this system the answer is FAILURE-RESOLVE-1 (a failing detector files its own item with root-cause suspects, so failed work becomes a fix). The metric, share of closed pull requests closed without merging, reads 0.36 (n = 100) against a target of <= 0.2. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-safety-by-limits-2026-S5 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

S6. One halt stops everything. Belief: an autonomous system cannot be stopped. Test: every registered loop has a server-side owner and closing probe, so one switch reaches each of them. [2] In this system the answer is HALT-1 (one worker variable or committed file stops every cron, webhook and workflow job). The metric, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, reads 1.0 (n = 112) against a target of >= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

## 6. Limitations

- Scale. One organization: 100 closed pull requests (64 merged) over 0.75 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 80% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Own r&d question set, regenerated from this system's records, version 2026-11-21; its findings may change in later versions.

## 7. Conclusion

On this system's records, 4 of 6 findings hold. The gaps are the system corrects itself when a limit is crossed; little work is thrown away.

That is evidence against the view that AI is safe only if a person approves every step: the properties tested here are engineering properties of the loop, and each can be measured and repaired without waiting on a better model.

The paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge, so a reader who returns later sees the current result, not this one.
